clinicalPearls: A congenitally small cornea (reduced horizontal diameter) in an eye that is otherwise of relatively normal size
It is distinct from microphthalmos, in which the whole globe is small, and from nanophthalmos
The cornea is usually clear and often flatter than normal, tending toward hyperopia
It may be isolated or associated with other anterior segment anomalies and syndromes
There is an increased long-term risk of angle-closure and other glaucoma
Management centres on refractive correction, amblyopia treatment and lifelong glaucoma surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Microcornea arises from arrest of corneal growth in the fifth month of gestation or from overgrowth of the surrounding optic cup rim, producing a cornea of reduced diameter. The small, often flat cornea reduces refractive power, typically causing hyperopia, and the associated crowded anterior segment anatomy predisposes to angle-closure glaucoma. It can occur in isolation or as part of anterior segment dysgenesis and various systemic syndromes, reflecting shared developmental pathways.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital glaucoma (which enlarges the cornea, the opposite finding)
Syndromic associations (for example with cataract or coloboma)
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of corneal diameter and axial length to distinguish from microphthalmos
Gonioscopy and intraocular pressure for glaucoma risk
Assessment for associated ocular and systemic anomalies
redFlags: Signs of angle-closure or other glaucoma
reference.prognosis: Isolated microcornea generally has good vision with refractive correction; the main long-term concern is glaucoma, and prognosis worsens with associated anomalies.
pitfalls: Missing associated anterior segment or systemic anomalies
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Correct the associated refractive error, commonly hyperopia, with spectacles or contact lenses
Detect and treat amblyopia early in children with refractive correction and occlusion (patching) therapy
Undertake lifelong glaucoma surveillance with intraocular pressure measurement and gonioscopy given the angle-closure risk
Treat established glaucoma with topical pressure-lowering agents, and consider laser peripheral iridotomy or surgery for angle closure
Screen for and manage associated anterior segment dysgenesis and systemic syndromic features
Provide long-term paediatric ophthalmology follow-up to safeguard visual development
